Conformal network link prediction with false discovery rate control under unstructured missingness

Wenqin Du ††thanks: Equal contribution.    Wanteng Ma11footnotemark: 1    Dong Xia    Yuan Zhang ††thanks: Corresponding author: mailto:yzhanghf@stat.osu.edu    Wen Zhou
University of Southern California1, University of Pennsylvania2,
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology3,
Ohio State University4, and New York University5
Abstract

We propose a new method for predicting multiple missing links in partially observed networks while controlling the false discovery rate (FDR), a largely unresolved challenge in network analysis. The main difficulty lies in handling complex dependencies and unknown missing patterns. We introduce conformal link prediction, a distribution-free procedure grounded in the exchangeability structure of weighted graphon models. Our approach constructs conformal p-values via a novel multi-splitting strategy that restores exchangeability within local test sets, thereby ensuring valid row-wise FDR control, even under unknown missing mechanisms. To achieve FDR control across all missing links, we further develop a new aggregation scheme based on e-values, which accommodates arbitrary dependence across network predictions. Our method requires no assumptions on the missing rates, applies to weighted, unweighted, undirected, and bipartite networks, and enjoys finite-sample theoretical guarantees. Extensive simulations and real-world data study confirm the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed approach.

1 Introduction

Link prediction (Janicik and Larrick, 2005; Clauset et al., 2008; Kim and Leskovec, 2011; Mohan and Pearl, 2021) is a fundamental problem in network data analysis, with applications in sociology, econometrics, and biology, where real-world networks are often only partially observed. While early work focused on accurately predicting individual links, the growing demand for simultaneous prediction of multiple links has brought concerns about reproducibility and statistical validity to the forefront. Framing this task as a multiple hypothesis testing problem has led to the adoption of false discovery rate (FDR) control as a key tool. However, FDR control for link prediction in networks presents unique challenges owing to complex edge dependencies and unknown, heterogeneous patterns of missingness. To address these challenges, which remain inadequately resolved in the literature, we introduce conformal link prediction (clp), a new method for simultaneous link prediction with provably FDR control.

Let 𝐀∈ℝn×n{\mathbf{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} denote the adjacency matrix of a directed network with nn nodes and no self-loops, where entries Ai,jA_{i,j} and Aj,iA_{j,i} are not necessarily equal. Missingness in 𝐀{\mathbf{A}} is described by a binary matrix 𝐌∈{0,1}n×n{\mathbf{M}}\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}, where its entry Mi,j=1M_{i,j}=1 if Ai,jA_{i,j} is missing, and 𝐌{\mathbf{M}} can be any deterministic or random binary matrix. We define 𝐌c=𝟏n×1​𝟏n×1T−𝐌{\mathbf{M}}^{c}=\bm{1}_{n\times 1}\bm{1}_{n\times 1}^{{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}}-{\mathbf{M}}. Throughout, we only adopt the following standard assumption.

Assumption 1.1 (Shao and Zhang (2023))

The missing pattern 𝐌{\mathbf{M}} is independent of the network, specified by the adjacency matrix 𝐀{\mathbf{A}}.

Assumption 1.1 is closely related to the classical missing-completely-at-random (MCAR) condition in the missing data literature (Rubin, 1976; Molenberghs et al., 2014; Little and Rubin, 2019). In our graphon setting, it requires the missingness pattern 𝐌{\mathbf{M}} to be independent of the realized network 𝐀{\mathbf{A}}, while still allowing heterogeneous or structured missing patterns. This differs from missing-at-random (MAR) mechanisms, where missingness may depend on the latent node variables {ξi}i=1n\{\xi_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} but not directly on the realized link values conditional on these latent variables. It also excludes missing-not-at-random (MNAR) mechanisms, where missingness may depend directly on the unobserved value Ai,jA_{i,j}.

We define the test set as the collection of unobserved links: 𝒟test:={(i,j):i,j∈[n]={1,…,n},Mi,j=1}{\cal D}_{\rm test}:=\{(i,j):i,j\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\},M_{i,j}=1\}, where 𝒟test{\cal D}_{\rm test} is random if 𝐌{\mathbf{M}} is random. For simplicity of presentation, we focus on predicting all links in 𝒟test{\cal D}_{\rm test}, while our method can be applied to any subset. Following Jin and Candès (2022), we formulate link prediction as a multiple testing problem with random hypotheses:

Hi,j:Ai,j≤ci,j​for ​(i,j)∈𝒟test,H_{i,j}:A_{i,j}\leq c_{i,j}~\text{for }(i,j)\in{\cal D}_{\rm test}, (1)

where ci,jc_{i,j}’s are user-specified. For example, in the international trade flow network (Helpman et al., 2008), if the goal is to determine whether any trading activity exists between two countries, ci,jc_{i,j} can be set to zero. Alternatively, if the focus is on detecting higher volumes of bilateral trade, ci,jc_{i,j} can be set to an appropriate positive value.

For the rejection set ℛ:={(i,j)∈𝒟test:Reject ​Hi,j}\mathcal{R}:=\{{(i,j)\in{\cal D}_{\rm test}}:\textrm{Reject }H_{i,j}\}, the false discovery proportion (FDP) is defined as FDP=(|ℛ|∨1)−1∑(i,j)∈ℛ𝟙[Ai,j≤ci,j]\textrm{FDP}=(|\mathcal{R}|\vee 1)^{-1}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{R}}\mathbbm{1}_{[A_{i,j}\leq c_{i,j}]}, based on given {ci,j}(i,j)∈𝒟test\{c_{i,j}\}_{(i,j)\in{\cal D}_{\rm test}} and observed data {𝐀∘𝐌c,𝐌}\big\{{\mathbf{A}}\circ{\mathbf{M}}^{c},{\mathbf{M}}\big\}, where “∘\circ” denotes the element-wise product. Our objective is to control the conditional FDR given 𝐌{\mathbf{M}} at a pre-specified significance level, and accordingly treating the test set as fixed. Clearly, the marginal FDR control is thus also valid since one can marginalize the conditional FDR control guarantee over 𝐌{\mathbf{M}}. Specifically, we define FDR=𝔼⁡(FDP|𝐌)\textrm{FDR}=\mathbb{E}(\textrm{FDP}|{\mathbf{M}}). A major challenge for FDR control in classical link prediction methods is that the unknown and potentially non-uniform missing patters lead to non-exchangeable observations 𝐀∘𝐌c{\mathbf{A}}\circ{\mathbf{M}}^{c}, which hinders uncertainty quantification. Moreover, complex dependencies among predicted links further render most traditional FDR control procedures inapplicable.

1.1 Related literature

Link prediction has been extensively studied over recent decades (Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg, 2003; Hasan and Zaki, 2011; Zhang et al., 2017). An alternative perspective treats the network as a random matrix or a realization of an unobservable graphon, leading to approaches based on matrix estimation or completion (Candès et al., 2011; Koltchinskii et al., 2011; Davenport et al., 2014) and graphon estimation (Gao et al., 2015; Xu, 2018). However, most existing studies either lack uncertainty quantification or rely on strong modeling assumptions. To achieve our goal of distribution-free uncertainty quantification, we bridge two key ingredients. The first is conformal prediction (Vovk et al., 2005), a powerful model-agnostic framework that enables flexible applications, including recent adaptations to multiple testing via the construction of conformal pp-values (Lei and Candès, 2021; Jin and Candès, 2022; Bates et al., 2023). The second ingredient is the e-BH procedure (Wang and Ramdas, 2022), which ensures valid FDR control under complex dependence among conformal pp-values. Based on e-values (Vovk and Wang, 2021), this procedure has proven effective in handling complex dependence among statistics, with recent successful applications in derandomized knockoffs (Ren and Barber, 2024) and e-value-based conformal prediction (Bashari et al., 2024; Ignatiadis et al., 2024).

Conformal prediction for matrix data was pioneered by Gui et al. (2023) and Shao and Zhang (2023). Gui et al. (2023) considered random missingness and is therefore more closely related to our setting, whereas Shao and Zhang (2023) examined arbitrary and potentially adversarial missing patterns. However, neither study addresses the task of predicting multiple links. Recently, Marandon (2024) introduced conformal link prediction with FDR control, but the method is limited to unweighted networks and assumes a “double-standard” sampling scheme, requiring uniform missing rates across all links. Under this assumption, subsequent work by Blanchard et al. (2024) sought to provide theoretical justification for Marandon (2024). This uniformity condition effectively imposes the exchangeability on all links with values exceeding ci,jc_{i,j}, simplifying the analysis but limiting practical applicability. Liang et al. (2024) proposed a structured splitting scheme for simultaneous prediction of a small number of links, without considering the multiple testing. Zhao et al. (2024) construct prediction intervals for individual links with marginal coverage guarantees, rather than controlling the FDR for multiple dependent links simultaneously. To date, valid FDR control for multiple link prediction under general network settings remains an open challenge.

1.2 Our contributions

We develop a new conformal inference framework for multiple network link prediction with provable FDR control. Unlike prior work, our method is tailored to the complex structure of partially observed networks, characterized by heterogeneous missingness and intricate dependencies among predictions. The approach combines novel conformal calibration schemes with a principled global aggregation strategy. Our main contributions are threefold.

First, we introduce a conformal inference method tailored to row-wise link prediction. A key innovation is a carefully constructed multi-splitting scheme that partitions each row’s test set and adaptively allocates calibration sets. This enables the construction of exchangeable nonconformity scores and valid conformal pp-values, even under unknown and nonuniform missingness. The method achieves FDR control for any node sizes nn through a nontrivial adaptation of the Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) procedure (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995), applied in a row-wise fashion.

Second, we propose a novel aggregation technique that transforms the row-wise test decisions, obtained via the BH procedure, into valid e-values, and applies the e-BH procedure for FDR control. This step requires careful design to accommodate unknown yet arbitrary dependence across predicted network links, a challenge not addressed by standard conformal or e-value methods. We further introduce a derandomization step to enhance stability, along with an e-value inflation strategy to improve power, both tailored to the unique demands for predicting multiple network links.

Third, our method is broadly applicable: it extends naturally to unweighted, undirected, and bipartite networks, requires no knowledge of the missingness mechanism, and provides finite-sample guarantees. Our framework advances the scope of conformal inference in network analysis, extending beyond existing approaches such as Tibshirani et al. (2019) and Gui et al. (2023). Numerical studies confirm the practical effectiveness of the proposed method.

2 Conformal link prediction with FDR control

2.1 Link prediction under unknown missing probabilities

We adopt the general weighted graphon model (Gao et al., 2016) as the base for our method for its flexibility and generality. We assume entry Ai,jA_{i,j} of the adjacency matrix 𝐀{\mathbf{A}} is drawn from a distribution parameterized by f⁡(ξi,ξj)f(\xi_{i},\xi_{j}), such as Bernoulli and Gaussian. That is,

Ai,j∼f⁡(ξi,ξj), for ​i≠j∈[n],where ​{ξi}1≤i≤n∼i.i.d.Uniform⁡[0,1].\displaystyle A_{i,j}\sim f(\xi_{i},\xi_{j}),\text{ ~for~ }i\neq j\in[n],~~\text{where }\{\xi_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm i.i.d.}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Uniform}[0,1]. (2)

Intuitively, model (2) first samples nodes independently from a hyper-population of “all kinds of nodes”, then generates links according to the function ff. This framework encompasses a broad class of network models, such as in the social relations model (Kenny and La Voie, 1984), the conditionally independent dyad model (Graham, 2020), and the random-effects model (Gelman and Hill, 2006).

Under model (2), for any permutation π⁡(⋅)\pi(\cdot) of node labels, we have

{Ai,j}i≠j∈[n]=d{Aπ⁡(i),π⁡(j)}i≠j∈[n],\{A_{i,j}\}_{i\neq j\in[n]}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\{A_{\pi(i),\pi(j)}\}_{i\neq j\in[n]}, (3)

which is known as the exchangeability property of 𝐀{\mathbf{A}}. Importantly, the exchangeability in (3) pertains to the not-fully-observable complete 𝐀{\mathbf{A}}, not the observed 𝐀∘𝐌c{\mathbf{A}}\circ{\mathbf{M}}^{c}. Note that our notion of exchangeability in (3) differs from that in prior work. Previous studies (Tibshirani et al., 2019; Gui et al., 2023) rely on exchangeability induced by the random 𝐌{\mathbf{M}} where they assume Mi,j∼Ber⁡(qi,j)M_{i,j}\sim\operatorname{Ber}(q_{i,j}), and therefore require either uniform missing rates qi,j{q_{i,j}} or their accurate estimations under the “weighted exchangeability” framework. In contrast, we model 𝐀{\mathbf{A}} as a random graph with inherent exchangeability as defined in (3). With the mild additional assumption of exchangeability of the complete 𝐀{\mathbf{A}}, we waive the need for prior knowledge of the potentially non-uniform missing rates qi,j{q_{i,j}}’s, a key restrictive assumption in earlier works.

To address the challenge of unknown missing patterns, we propose a divide-and-conquer approach to break the problem into sub-tasks. First, for each row i0i_{0}, we construct “local tests” where exchangeability holds within a row-wise subset of observations, which leads to valid “local” FDR controls. Then, the local test decisions are aggregated into e-values to construct an aggregated test of the hypotheses in (1) for all unobserved links, with valid FDR control.

Our first step is to design a local test, which focuses only on row i0i_{0}, by constructing exchangeable conformal pp-values (Jin and Candès, 2022). Let ℐtesti0={(i0,j):j∈[n],Mi0,j=1}{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}=\{(i_{0},j):j\in[n],M_{i_{0},j}=1\} denote the column indices of missing entries in row i0i_{0}, corresponding to missing links for node i0i_{0}. Hi0,j:Ai0,j≤ci0,j,for ​j∈ℐtesti0.H_{i_{0},j}:A_{i_{0},j}\leq c_{i_{0},j},~~\text{for }j\in{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}. (4)

In presence of ties, one can simply apply a random tie-breaking trick as that in Lei et al. (2018); Tibshirani et al. (2019).

2.3 Construction of 𝐀^\widehat{\mathbf{A}} and local tests with FDR control

To build an operational method, we construct 𝐀^\widehat{\mathbf{A}} that satisfies (5) for implementing the local test in Section 2.2. Due to the unknown missingness, directly applying popular existing link prediction methods, such as matrix factorization or node similarity-based tools, would fail the required exchangeabililty condition in (5). To better illustrate our strategy, we start with an “oracle method”. Consider a weighed link estimation:

Proposition 2.3 (Conditional independence of empirical pp-values)

For network 𝐀{\mathbf{A}} generated from (2), under Assumption 1.1, conditional on {ξj:j∈ℐtraini0}\{\xi_{j}:j\in{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}\}, {Ai,j:i,j∈ℐtraini0}\{A_{i,j}:i,j\in{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}\} and the missing pattern 𝐌{\mathbf{M}}, the pp-values in (13) are independent within ℐtesti0​(k0){\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}(k_{0}).

Theorem 2.4 (FDR control for the local test with empirical pp-values by splitting)

Under model (2) and Assumption 1.1, for any αBH∈(0,1)\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}\in(0,1), conditional on 𝐌{\mathbf{M}}, the output ℛBHi0,k0​(αBH)\mathcal{R}_{\rm BH}^{i_{0},k_{0}}(\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}) of Algorithm 1 for testing (9) satisfies FDR ≤αBH\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}} for testing (9).

2.4 Step 2: aggregating local tests for FDR control

Recall that we break down the original problem in two stages: from an aggregated test to local tests, one for each row; then, within each row, we further break down the local test by partitioning ℐtesti0{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}} into disjoint subsets. We now aggregate the results of the local tests to devise an aggregated rejection set with valid FDR control for predicting all missing links. To this end, we leverage the e-BH procedure (Wang and Ramdas, 2022; Ren and Barber, 2024).

The e-BH procedure offers a notable advantage that its validity requires only that each individual e-value satisfies 𝔼⁡(ei0,j)≤1\mathbb{E}(e_{i_{0},j})\leq 1 under the null hypotheses in (9), without any assumptions on their dependence structure. The central idea of our aggregated test is to rescale the binary test decision functions from the local tests into valid e-values. Using the leave-one-out analysis of the BH procedure (Ferreira and Zwinderman, 2006), we show that 𝔼[𝟙{j∈ℛBHi0,k0(αBH)}/{|ℛBHi0,k0(αBH)|∨1}]≤αBH/|ℐtesti0(k0)|\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbbm{1}\{j\in\mathcal{R}_{\rm BH}^{i_{0},k_{0}}(\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}})\}/\{|\mathcal{R}_{\rm BH}^{i_{0},k_{0}}(\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}})|\vee 1\}\big]\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}/|{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}(k_{0})|, for each jj. Therefore, for j∈ℐtesti0​(k0)j\in{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}(k_{0}),

ei0,j:=|ℐtesti0(k0)|⋅𝟙{j∈ℛBHi0,k0(αBH)}{|ℛBHi0,k0​(αBH)|∨1}⋅αBH\displaystyle e_{i_{0},j}:=\frac{|{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}(k_{0})|\cdot\mathbbm{1}\{j\in\mathcal{R}_{\rm BH}^{i_{0},k_{0}}(\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}})\}}{\{|\mathcal{R}_{\rm BH}^{i_{0},k_{0}}(\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}})|\vee 1\}\cdot\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}} (14)

is a valid e-value, namely, 𝔼⁡(ei0,j)≤1\mathbb{E}(e_{i_{0},j})\leq 1 under the null Hi0,jH_{i_{0},j} in (4). Then, by separately applying the e-BH procedure to {ei0,j,j∈ℐtesti0​(k0)}\{e_{i_{0},j},j\in{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}(k_{0})\}, one could obtain a local test for each row i0i_{0} with the FDR controlled at level αBH\alpha_{\rm BH}. But here, we would directly construct an aggregated test using all {ei,j:(i,j)∈𝒟test}\{e_{i,j}:(i,j)\in{\cal D}_{\rm test}\}. To this end, we sort all e-values {ei,j:(i,j)∈𝒟test}\{e_{i,j}:(i,j)\in{\cal D}_{\rm test}\} in descending order: e(1)≥⋯≥e(|𝒟test|)e_{(1)}\geq\cdots\geq e_{(|{\cal D}_{\rm test}|)}. Then, for any given αeBH>0\alpha_{\mathrm{eBH}}>0, set

k^:=max{k:1≤k≤|𝒟test|,e(k)≥|𝒟test|αeBH​k} or k^=0 if the set is empty,\displaystyle\widehat{k}:=\max\left\{k:1\leq k\leq|{\cal D}_{\rm test}|,e_{(k)}\geq\frac{|{\cal D}_{\rm test}|}{\alpha_{\mathrm{eBH}}k}\right\}~\text{ or }~\widehat{k}=0\text{ if the set is empty}, (15)

and reject all Hi,jH_{i,j}’s with e-values ei,j≥e(k^)e_{i,j}\geq e_{(\widehat{k})}. The procedure fails to reject any hypotheses when k^=0\widehat{k}=0. This rejection rule controls FDR of (1) at the level αeBH\alpha_{\mathrm{eBH}}.

To mitigate variations arising from the random selection of ℐcalibi0{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}} and ℐtraini0{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}, we further adopt a derandomization procedure (Ren and Barber, 2024). This builds on the property that the average of multiple e-values remains a valid e-value (Vovk and Wang, 2021). For each row i0i_{0} and j∈ℐtesti0​(k0)j\in{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}(k_{0}), we repeat Algorithm 1 for mi0m_{i_{0}} times and compute the e-values ei0,j(1),…,ei0,j(mi0)e_{i_{0},j}^{(1)},\ldots,e_{i_{0},j}^{(m_{i_{0}})}. Then we derandomize the e-values as follows:

e¯i0,j:=1mi0​∑l=1mi0ei0,j(l),where ​j∈ℐtesti0​(k0).\displaystyle\bar{e}_{i_{0},j}:=\frac{1}{m_{i_{0}}}\sum_{l=1}^{m_{i_{0}}}e_{i_{0},j}^{(l)},~~\text{where }j\in{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}(k_{0}). (16)

Finally, we apply the e-BH procedure to all e¯i,j\bar{e}_{i,j}’s as in (15), using them in the same manner as ei,je_{i,j} in the original algorithm described above. This yields our method clp, summarized in Algorithm 2, which enjoys finite-sample valid FDR control as shown in Theorem 2.5.

Theorem 2.5 (FDR control of clp for testing (1))

Under the conditions of Theorem 2.4, given any αeBH∈(0,1)\alpha_{\mathrm{eBH}}\in(0,1) and for any choice of αBH∈(0,1)\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}\in(0,1), conditional on 𝐌{\mathbf{M}}, the rejection set produced by Algorithm 2 satisfies FDR ≤αeBH\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{eBH}}.

We make two key remarks. First, our method clp accommodates arbitrary missing mechanism, provided Assumption 1.1 hold. Examples include: (1) random but non-uniform missingness (Gui et al., 2023), and (2) structured missingness, such as block or staggered patterns commonly encountered in panel data (Athey et al., 2021; Xiong and Pelger, 2023). Second, as shown in Theorem 2.5, clp guarantees valid FDR control for any choice of αBH\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}, while Ren and Barber (2024) recommend setting αBH=αeBH/2\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}=\alpha_{\mathrm{eBH}}/2 for improved powers.

We note that our method may exhibit some conservativeness in practice. By (14), the maximum possible value of ei0,je_{i_{0},j} for j∈ℐtesti0​(k0)j\in{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}(k_{0}) is |ℐtesti0​(k0)|/αBH|{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}(k_{0})|/\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}. Thus, when |ℐtesti0​(k0)||{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}(k_{0})| is small due to extensive data-splitting, the resulting e-values may be lowered, limiting the number of rejections under the e-BH procedure in (15). To alleviate this effect, we introduce an inflation factor to adjust each e-value ei,je_{i,j} and increase the likelihood of rejection. Numerical studies in Section 3 explore distinct choices of this inflation factor and suggest that using a factor of 1/αBH1/\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}} effectively enhances power while maintaining well-controlled FDR. A more rigorous theoretical characterization of this practically effective factor remains an intriguing yet challenging direction for future work.

Computing the dissimilarity measure in (11) is computationally intensive due to the evaluation of all terms d^j1,j2,j\widehat{d}_{j_{1},j_{2},j} in (10). The overall computational complexity of clp is O⁡(m​|ℐtraini0|2​|ℐcalibi0|)O\big(m|{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}|^{2}|{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}|\big), where mm is the number of missing entries, assuming |ℐtraini0||{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}| (and |ℐcalibi0||{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}|) are of the same order across all i0∈[n]i_{0}\in[n]. Specifically, computing (10) and (11) incurs a cost of O⁡(|ℐtraini0|)O\big(|{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}|\big), while the aggregation step in (12) adds additional O⁡(|ℐcalibi0|)O\big(|{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}|). In practice, our method can be accelerated by reducing the sizes of ℐtraini0{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}} and ℐcalibi0{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}; for instance, setting ℐtraini0≍ℐcalibi0=O⁡(1){\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}\asymp{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}=O(1) reduces the overall complexity to O⁡(m)O(m), though at the potential cost of reduced accuracy in estimating dissimilarity and, consequently, lower power.

2.5 Extensions and comparisons

While our proposed framework is detailed for directed networks, it naturally extends to bipartite and undirected networks with minimal modifications. The adaptation to bipartite networks is straightforward, owing to the their exchangeability. That is, we can use more rows to construct A^i0,j\widehat{A}_{i_{0},j} and the associated pp-values. Extending to undirected networks requires extra care due to the symmetry constraints Ai,j=Aj,iA_{i,j}=A_{j,i} and Mi,j=Mj,iM_{i,j}=M_{j,i}, but the solution is remarkably simple. We first apply our Algorithms 1 and 2 up to Line 9 of Algorithm 2, where the e¯i,j\bar{e}_{i,j} values are obtained. Thereafter, we apply the remainder of Algorithm 2, the e-BH procedure, only to the upper triangular part, i.e., {e¯i,j:(i,j)∈𝒟test​ and ​i<j}\{\bar{e}_{i,j}:(i,j)\in{\cal D}_{\rm test}\text{ and }i<j\}, instead of the full set {e¯i,j:(i,j)∈𝒟test}\{\bar{e}_{i,j}:(i,j)\in{\cal D}_{\rm test}\}. Formal algorithmic descriptions (Algorithms 3 and 4) and theoretical justifications for both extensions are provided in Section D of the Supplementary Material.

We conclude this section by comparing our method with existing works. Gui et al. (2023) considers arbitrary 𝐀{\mathbf{A}} under a missing-at-random mechanism but requires knowledge of, or accurate estimates for, the odds ratios introduced by missing probabilities. In contrast, we allow arbitrary missingness patterns 𝐌{\mathbf{M}} that are independent of 𝐀{\mathbf{A}}, and leverage the latent graphon structure in 𝐀{\mathbf{A}} to reinstate the exchangeability. This enables our method to accommodate a broader class of missing mechanisms. Overall, the two approaches rely on different assumptions and do not subsume each other. We also note that our paper considers random matrices 𝐀{\mathbf{A}}, whereas in related work such as Gui et al. (2023); Liang et al. (2024), the matrix to be tested is treated as fixed. More recently, Marandon (2024); Blanchard et al. (2024) proposed a novel FDR control approach that casts link prediction as a classification problem. While innovative, their formulation is inherently limited to unweighted networks and assumes missingness rates take only two distinct values, depending on whether an entry is 00 or 11. In contrast, our method applies to both weighted and unweighted networks and allows fully heterogeneous, unknown missingness rates, offering greater flexibility in practice. It is also possible to leverage general p-to-e calibrators (Shafer et al., 2011; Vovk and Wang, 2021) to construct the e-values, but as reported in literature, this approach tends to be rather conservative. We leave further studies along this line to future research.

3 Simulations

3.1 Simulation 1: Tuning our algorithm

We generate networks following the distribution Ai,j=f⁡(ξi,ξj)+ϵi,jA_{i,j}=f(\xi_{i},\xi_{j})+\epsilon_{i,j}, where ϵi,j∼Uniform⁡[−0.1,0.1]\epsilon_{i,j}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[-0.1,0.1]. Three graphons are considered to cover a wide range of scenarios:

(i) Setting 1 (low-rank and smooth): f1​(ξi,ξj)=ξi3+2​ξj3f_{1}(\xi_{i},\xi_{j})=\xi_{i}^{3}+2\xi_{j}^{3};

(ii) Setting 2 (high-rank): f2​(ξi,ξj)=max⁡(ξi,ξj)23​cos⁡[0.1/{(2​ξi−1/2)3+(ξj−1/2)3+0.01}]f_{2}(\xi_{i},\xi_{j})=\max(\xi_{i},\xi_{j})^{\frac{2}{3}}\cos[0.1/\{(2\xi_{i}-1/2)^{3}+(\xi_{j}-1/2)^{3}+0.01\}];

(iii) Setting 3 (non-smooth): f3​(ξi,ξj)=(3​ξi2+ξj2)⋅cos⁡{(2​ξi4+ξj4)−1}f_{3}(\xi_{i},\xi_{j})=(3\xi_{i}^{2}+\xi_{j}^{2})\cdot\cos\{{(2\xi_{i}^{4}+\xi_{j}^{4})}^{-1}\}.

We fix the network size at n=200n=200 and set the proportion of missing links to 0.20.2, resulting in an average of 3,9803,980 missing links. Specifically, we generate Mi,j∼M_{i,j}\sim Bernoulli(qi,j)(q_{i,j}) and consider heterogeneous missing probabilities, where qi,jq_{i,j}’s are independently generated from Uniform⁡[0,0.4]\mathrm{Uniform}[0,0.4]. We set the null hypotheses to be true, namely ci,j=Ai,jc_{i,j}=A_{i,j} in (1), for 7070% of entries. For the remaining 30%30\%, we set ci,j=Ai,j−1.5c_{i,j}=A_{i,j}-1.5. For each row i0i_{0}, all observed entries are randomly split into ℐtraini0∪ℐcalibi0{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}\cup{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}} with a ratio of |ℐtraini0|:|ℐcalibi0|=2:3|{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}|:|{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}|=2:3, and we set αBH=αeBH/2\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}=\alpha_{\mathrm{eBH}}/2 following Ren and Barber (2024). In the BH procedure, we choose r0=25r_{0}=25, as defined in the paragraph following (9). We use the Gaussian kernel K(x)=exp(−x2/2)/2​πK(x)=\exp\big(-x^{2}/2\big)/\sqrt{2\pi} in (12) and derandomize local tests using 2020 repetitions in (16).

Recall that in (14), we inflate the e-values by a factor of c/αBHc/\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}. Here, we examine the impact of c∈{0.5,1,1.5}c\in\{0.5,1,1.5\}. Performance is evaluated using the FDR, approximated by the averaged FDP, and power, both assessed over 100100 experiments. We vary αeBH\alpha_{\mathrm{eBH}} from 0.10.1 to 0.30.3. The results in Figure 3 show that our method consistently controls the empirical FDR across significance levels when c=0.5c=0.5, and in most settings when c=1c=1. It also achieves desirable power results as αeBH\alpha_{\mathrm{eBH}} increases. Overall, we recommend c=1c=1 as it strike a satisfactory balance between FDR control and decent power.

3.2 Simulation 2: Comparison with benchmark methods

We compare our method (clp) with conformal matrix completion (cmc, Gui et al. (2023)) and the link prediction method by Marandon (2024) (dss) via two sub-simulations for weighted and unweighted networks, respectively. While cmc applies to both settings, dss is, by design, primarily suited for unweighted networks.

For the first sub-simulation (weighted links), we adopt Settings 1–3 from Section 3.1, fixing αBH=0.1\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}=0.1 and αeBH=0.2\alpha_{\mathrm{eBH}}=0.2. The threshold ci​jc_{ij} is set as a specific quantile of the observed link weights, with the quantile level κ\kappa varying from 0.10.1 to 0.50.5. As noted earlier, we inflate the e-values in (14) by a factor of 1/αBH1/\alpha_{\text{BH}}. Note that cmc only provides confidence intervals with guaranteed coverage, rather than pp-values. Its underlying idea is to approximate the population quantiles of absolute prediction errors by the empirical quantiles of calibrated absolute errors, a procedure valid only for two-sided problems. To adapt it to our one-sided multiple testing problem (1), we modify it to produce comparable pp-values: we omit the absolute value when computing errors and construct the empirical distribution function F^eCDF​(⋅)\widehat{F}_{\text{eCDF}}(\cdot) based on the calibrated errors A^i​j−Ai​j\widehat{A}_{ij}-A_{ij}. We then compute pp-values for cmc as 1−F^eCDF​(A^i​j−ci​j),(i,j)∈𝒟test1-\widehat{F}_{\text{eCDF}}(\widehat{A}_{ij}-c_{ij}),(i,j)\in{\cal D}_{\rm test}, and apply the BH procedure. Note also that cmc requires a hypothesized rank as input. In practice, results of cmc are robust to the hypothesized rank, as also noted by Gui et al. (2023). Accordingly, we fix the rank at r=2r=2 for cmc across all settings for demonstration.

As shown in Figure 4, while both clp and cmc control the FDR, clp consistently achieves higher power across all settings. We note that cmc is sensitive to the choice of ci,jc_{i,j} values. In Section B of the Supplementary Material, we adopt the approach in Section 3.1 to select ci,jc_{i,j} based on signal strength. Under such configuration, cmc fails to control the FDR, whereas clp continues to perform well.

To compare with dss, we set up a second sub-simulation for unweighted networks, using a different network-generating process from that used for the weighted case. Specifically, we generate Ai,j=𝟙{(ξi+ξj)/2+ϵi,j>t}A_{i,j}=\mathbbm{1}\{(\xi_{i}+\xi_{j})/2+\epsilon_{i,j}>t\}, where ϵi,j∼Uniform⁡[−0.25,0.25]\epsilon_{i,j}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[-0.25,0.25]. We set ci,j=0.5c_{i,j}=0.5 in (1) and vary t∈{0,0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2}t\in\{0,0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2\} to control the number of null and alternative hypotheses. We consider heterogeneous missingness by drawing qi,j∼Uniform⁡[0,0.2]q_{i,j}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[0,0.2] independently for each (i,j)(i,j), yielding an average proportion of missing links of approximately 10%10\%. We fix αBH=0.2\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}=0.2 and αeBH=0.2\alpha_{\mathrm{eBH}}=0.2, and use r0=50r_{0}=50 to improve estimation of Ai,jA_{i,j} for unweighted networks.

As displayed in Figure 5, all three methods control the FDR across different values of tt. The conservativeness of cmc aligns with our observation for weighted networks. While the FDR of dss exceeds that of clp, its relative low power can be attributed to the heterogeneous missing probabilities. In general, both clp and dss outperform cmc in the unweighted network setting, and our method demonstrates strong performance across both weighted and unweighted networks.

4 Data example: bilateral trade flows

We consider the bilateral trade flow data from Helpman et al. (2008), which records trade volumes between 158158 countries in 1989. The dataset forms a directed network, where both indices ii and jj represent countries acting as exporters and importers, respectively. The outcome Ai,j{A_{i,j}} denotes the log-transformed trade volume from country ii to country jj, with a mean of 3.823.82, standard deviation of 4.694.69, and a range from 00 to 18.3918.39. Here, Ai,j=0A_{i,j}=0 indicates no recorded trade flow. We randomly mask 10%10\% of the links, corresponding 2,4962,496 trade entries, for evaluating the prediction performance of different methods. For these held-out entries, we set ci,j=0.2c_{i,j}=0.2 in the random hypotheses (1), resulting in approximately equal proportion of null and alternative hypotheses.

We compare our method only with cmc, as the method dss is not applicable because it is classification-based and limited to binary or categorical links. Following our simulation setup, we implement clp with |ℐtraini0|:|ℐcalibi0|=2:3|{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}|:|{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}|=2:3 for each i0∈[n]i_{0}\in[n], set r0=25r_{0}=25, and use αBH=αeBH/2\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}}=\alpha_{\mathrm{eBH}}/2. We employ a Gaussian kernel for K⁡(⋅)K(\cdot) in (8) and perform 2020 derandomizations in (16). The nominal FDR level α\alpha is varied over {0.1,0.2,0.3}\{0.1,0.2,0.3\}.

The left panel of Figure 6 shows that clp controls FDR well across all the nominal FDR levels, whereas cmc substantially inflates the FDP. The right panel demonstrates that our method is also more powerful than cmc. As α\alpha increases, the empirical power of clp improves, and its advantage over cmc becomes more pronounced.

5 Concluding remarks

In this article, we develop a general framework for FDR control in multiple network link prediction, leveraging e-values and insights from conformal inference. We propose data-driven methods and a multiple-splitting strategy to reinstate the exchangeability required for computing nonconformity scores under complex network edge dependencies and heterogeneous missingness. With supporting theories, we establish performance guarantees for multiple link prediction without requiring knowledge of the underlying network distribution.

Experiments on both simulated and real data suggest that a 1/αBH1/\alpha_{\mathrm{BH}} inflation factor performs well for clp. Setting a conservative threshold for e-values in the e-BH procedure may be inefficient in practice. Blier-Wong and Wang (2024) proposed some preliminary strategies for boosting e-values in the e-BH procedure under certain distributional assumptions while maintaining FDR control. It is of interest to investigate whether an optimal inflation criterion of e-values exists in our context, and if so, how it can be effectively designed.

We note that block-wise schemes may be designed to offer computational savings. However, such approaches are challenging in our setting, as the required block-level exchangeability is fragile under random missingness in 𝐌{\mathbf{M}}. Missing entries can break the symmetry needed for valid permutation or aggregation, making it difficult to construct blocks that both satisfy exchangeability and remain robust to heterogeneous missingness patterns. Moreover, forming blocks using only observed entries limits their applicability for testing missingness itself. We leave a rigorous treatment of block-wise aggregation under missingness to future work.

Supplementary Material for
“Conformal network link prediction with false discovery rate control under unstructured missingness”

This Supplementary Material contains proofs of Theorems 2.2–2.5 and Propositions 2.1–2.3 in Section A. Additional results of numerical studies are provided in Section B for simulations and Section C for real data application. The extensions of our proposed method clp to undirected and bipartite networks are given in Section D. Additional results for Bernoulli missing patterns are given in Section E. Unless stated otherwise, all the notation follows the same definitions as in the main body of the paper.

Appendix B Additional numerical studies

We explore how signal strength affect the performance of clp, cmc and dss. For weighted network setting, we apply the graphons in Section 3.1, setting ci,j=Ai,j−δc_{i,j}=A_{i,j}-\delta for 3030% of the hypotheses and set ci,j=Ai,jc_{i,j}=A_{i,j} for the rest as the null hypothesis. Here, δ\delta controls signal strength.

Figure B.1 shows the empirical FDR and power across different values of signal strength δ\delta. As can be seen, cmc fails to control the FDR across all settings. Comparing the results in Figure B.1 and Figure 4, we see that the performance of cmc is sensitive to the choice of ci​jc_{ij}’s. In contrast, clp consistently achieves desirable FDR control and its power increases as the signal strength becomes larger across all settings.

Since the signal strength is not straightforward to define in the unweighted setting, we slightly modify our testing target to illustrate how signal strength affects the performance of different methods. Specifically, we generate pi,j∗=f⁡(ξi,ξj)+ϵi,jp^{*}_{i,j}=f(\xi_{i},\xi_{j})+\epsilon_{i,j} with the graphon functions in Settings 1–3 and rescale them by pi,j=(pi,j∗−mini,j⁡pi,j∗)/(maxi,j⁡pi,j∗−mini,j⁡pi,j∗)p_{i,j}=(p^{*}_{i,j}-\min_{i,j}p^{*}_{i,j})/(\max_{i,j}p^{*}_{i,j}-\min_{i,j}p^{*}_{i,j}) to [0,1][0,1]-valued probabilities. Then we independently generate Ai,j∼Bernoulli​(pi,j)A_{i,j}\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p_{i,j}). Different from the previous settings, here we consider heterogeneous missing probabilities where qi,jq_{i,j}’s are independently generated from Uniform⁡[0,0.4]\mathrm{Uniform}[0,0.4]. Instead of testing whether there is a true link or not, we test Hi,j:pi,j≤ci,jH_{i,j}:p_{i,j}\leq c_{i,j} for the random pi,jp_{i,j}’s, and set ci,j=pi,j−δc_{i,j}=p_{i,j}-\delta for 30% of the hypotheses regarding the missing entries. Otherwise, we set ci,j=pi,jc_{i,j}=p_{i,j} for the null hypotheses.

As shown in Figure B.2, clp and dss control FDR throughout the three settings, while cmc fails. Additionally, the relative low power of dss compared to clp can be attributed to the heterogeneous missing probabilities. Marandon (2024) assumes that the missingness rates qi,jq_{i,j}’s take only two distinct values, depending on whether the links are 00 or 11. The target of testing random pi,jp_{i,j}’s instead of Ai,jA_{i,j}’s can also contribute to dss making fewer rejections.

B.1 Comparison with dss under weighted networks

Note that the procedure in Marandon (2024) (dss) cannot be easily extended to weighted network settings with heterogeneous null values ci,jc_{i,j}, since their Dtrain0D_{\rm train}^{0} (the set of observed non-existent edges) and Dtrain1D_{\rm train}^{1} (the set of observed true edges) are not well-defined when ci,jc_{i,j} differs across missing entries. Furthermore, in Settings 11–33 introduced in Section 3.1 of the main paper, where the ci,jc_{i,j}’s are uniform, one way to apply the procedure in Marandon (2024) to test Hi,j:Ai,j≤ci,j​for ​(i,j)∈𝒟test,H_{i,j}:A_{i,j}\leq c_{i,j}~\text{for }(i,j)\in{\cal D}_{\rm test}, is as follows: during testing, we first transform the observed weighted network into an unweighted network using the threshold ci,jc_{i,j} (set to the quantile of the observed links in Settings 11–33). We then apply the procedure in Marandon (2024) to this transformed unweighted network.

The results are shown in Figure B.3. We observe that the procedure in Marandon (2024) fails to control the FDR. This can be attributed to the heterogeneous missing probabilities in Settings 11–33, which are not addressed by their method, as it assumes homogeneous missing probabilities.

B.2 Sensitivity of cmc to the choice of hypothesized rank

For the cmc method, we conducted additional experiments using a larger hypothesized rank, namely r=10r=10, under Settings 1–3 introduced in Section 3.1 of the main paper. As shown in Figure B.4, the performance of cmc with r=10r=10 is similar to that with r=2r=2 in these settings, in terms of both empirical FDR and power. As noted by Gui et al. (2023), in practice, results of cmc are robust to the hypothesized rank. Therefore, the performance of cmc shown in Figure B.4 can be attributed to the inherent robustness of the cmc method and that in Settings 11–33, increasing rr to 1010 may not alter the ability to recover the core low-dimensional signal in the network.

B.3 Weighted and unweighted estimators in clp

Recall that in Section 2.3 of the main paper, we construct a “fine-grained weighted estimator” of 𝐀{\mathbf{A}} through the weights w⁡(j1,j2),w(j_{1},j_{2}), which are determined by a dissimilarity measure d⁡(j1,j2)d(j_{1},j_{2}). The purpose of this construction is to preserve the relevant exchangeability structure while improving the estimation accuracy of 𝐀^\widehat{{\mathbf{A}}}. A natural question is that whether one could instead use an unweighted estimator, that is, an estimator with constant weights, and thereby pursue a trade-off between estimator simplicity and the estimation accuracy. The answer is yes. In fact, the unweighted estimator can be viewed as a special case of our general construction. Specifically, if we take d⁡(j1,j2)≡1,d(j_{1},j_{2})\equiv 1, then the resulting weight becomes w⁡(j1,j2)=1|ℐtraini0|,w(j_{1},j_{2})=\frac{1}{|{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}|}, which is constant over j2∈ℐtraini0j_{2}\in{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}. Hence, the corresponding estimator is unweighted. Moreover, the exchangeability argument underlying our clp procedure continues to apply in this case. Therefore, from a validity perspective, the unweighted estimator is also admissible.

However, using constant weights may substantially degrade the estimation accuracy of 𝐀^\widehat{\mathbf{A}}, which may consequently reduce power. To illustrate this trade-off, we conduct additional simulations comparing the weighted estimator and the unweighted estimator. We consider both a weighted-network setting and an unweighted-network setting. For the weighted-network setting, we use Setting 3 in Section 3.1 of the main paper. For the unweighted-network setting, we use the data-generating mechanism introduced in Section 3.2. In both cases, we apply clp with the same implementation as in the main paper, including the 1/αBH1/\alpha_{\rm BH} inflation factor for the e-values. Figure B.5 reports the empirical FDR and power for the two estimators. We present our original clp results using the “fine-grained weighted estimator”, shown in blue and labeled as the “weighted estimator”. For comparison, the results using the “unweighted estimator” sets d⁡(j1,j2)≡1d\left(j_{1},j_{2}\right)\equiv 1, as discussed above. Its performance is shown in orange. Under the weighted-network setting, the weighted estimator and the unweighted estimator perform similarly. Under the unweighted-network setting, the weighted estimator yields better power than the unweighted estimator, while still maintaining FDR control. These results suggest that although the unweighted estimator is valid and conceptually simpler, the fine-grained weighted estimator can have better power performance in practice.

B.4 Sensitivity of clp to the choice of r0r_{0}

In our construction, the e-value for j∈ℐtesti0​(k0)j\in\mathcal{I}_{\text{test}}^{i_{0}}(k_{0}) contains the factor |ℐtesti0​(k0)||\mathcal{I}_{\text{test}}^{i_{0}}(k_{0})| in the numerator, and the BH rejection set used in its denominator is also computed within this local test set. Therefore, the choice of r1r_{1}, which controls the upper bound on |ℐtesti0​(k0)||\mathcal{I}_{\text{test}}^{i_{0}}(k_{0})|, can affect the magnitude of the resulting e-values and hence the empirical performance of the final e-BH procedure. Specifically, a larger size of the local test set (larger r1r_{1}) may inflate e-values and potentially increase power, but it also reduces the size of each calibration subset ℐcalibi0​(j0)\mathcal{I}_{\text{calib}}^{i_{0}}(j_{0}), which may lead to more conservative conformal p-values in the BH procedure. Recall that in our clp implementation, r1r_{1} is determined by the calibration split size |ℐcalibi0||{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}| and r0r_{0} through r1:=⌊|ℐcalibi0|/r0⌋r_{1}:=\lfloor|\mathcal{I}_{\text{calib}}^{i_{0}}|/r_{0}\rfloor. Therefore, r1r_{1} is not an entirely independent tuning parameter, but can be tuned indirectly through r0r_{0}, where a larger value of r0r_{0} corresponds to a smaller r1r_{1}.

To examine the sensitivity of clp to the choice of r0r_{0} (and hence r1r_{1}), we conducted additional experiments under Settings 1–3 from Section 3.1 of the main paper. We set κ=0.3\kappa=0.3 and vary r0∈{10,20,30,40}r_{0}\in\{10,20,30,40\}. The results are shown in Figure B.6.

Across all three settings, the empirical FDR remains below the nominal level for all values of r0r_{0} considered, confirming that FDR control is robust to this choice. Additionally, the empirical power in Settings 1 and 2 increases slightly as r0r_{0} increases, while in Setting 3 it remains nearly unchanged. Overall, these results suggest that the performance of our method is not sensitive to the local test set size over the considered range, and that r0=25r_{0}=25 as used in the main paper provides a reasonable default.

Appendix C Additional real data analysis

In Section 4, we set ci,j=0.2c_{i,j}=0.2 and vary α∈{0.1,0.2,0.3}\alpha\in\{0.1,0.2,0.3\}. In this section, we fix α=0.2\alpha=0.2 and vary the value of ci,jc_{i,j} to further demonstrate the performance of clp and cmc. Specifically, we consider ci,j∈{0.2,2,4.3,7.1}c_{i,j}\in\{0.2,2,4.3,7.1\}, with the proportion of alternative hypotheses gradually decreasing to approximately 30%. The empirical FDR and power (averaging across 100100 independent runs) are summarised in Figure C.1. As expected, clp achieves valid FDR control across all configurations, while cmc does not. Moreover, as ci,jc_{i,j} becomes larger, the power of both methods decreases. As a result, clp performs well in detecting whether trading activity exists between two countries but becomes less powerful when detecting higher volumes of bilateral trade.

Appendix D FDR control for undirected and bipartite networks

In this section, we extend the proposed clp framework to accommodate undirected and bipartite networks, elaborating on the modified version of Algorithm 1. Notice that once Algorithm 1 and its properties are still valid to control the FDR for the local test as defined in Theorem 2.4, we can directly incorporate it into Algorithm 2 and establish the FDR control across all missing links by applying the proof of Theorem 2.5.

We start with the undirected networks. Due to symmetry, we consider that information on the network and missing patterns is incorporated in the upper triangular part, i.e. , {Ai,j}\{A_{i,j}\}, {Mi,j}\{M_{i,j}\}, for i<ji<j. To facilitate the analysis, we write the extended version of 𝐀{\mathbf{A}}, 𝐌{\mathbf{M}} as 𝐀′{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime}, 𝐌′{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}, where

Ai,j′={Ai,j if ​i<jAj,i if ​i>j;Mi,j′={Mi,j if ​i<jMj,i if ​i>j.A_{i,j}^{\prime}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}A_{i,j}&\text{ if }{i<j}\\ A_{j,i}&\text{ if }{i>j}\end{array}\right.~~;\quad M_{i,j}^{\prime}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}M_{i,j}&\text{ if }{i<j}\\ M_{j,i}&\text{ if }{i>j}\end{array}\right.. (D.1)

We now describe the FDR control for the local test in undirected networks in Alogrihtm 3.

Proposition D.1 (Conditional independence in undirected networks)

Suppose we run Algorithm 1 on 𝐀′{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime} and 𝐌′{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}, with the test set 𝒟test{\cal D}_{\rm test} in the upper triangular matrix. Then, conditional on {ξj:j∈ℐtraini0}\{\xi_{j}:j\in{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}\}, {Ai,j:i,j∈ℐtraini0,i<j}\{A_{i,j}:i,j\in{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}},{i<j}\} and the missing pattern 𝐌{\mathbf{M}}, the p-values in (13) from 𝐀′{\mathbf{A}}^{\prime} and 𝐌′{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime} are valid and independent within ℐtesti0​(k0){\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}(k_{0}).

Figure D.1 provides an illustrative example of the splitting procedure in clp for an undirected network. It is seen that the construction follows the same procedure as described in Section 2.2 for directed networks. Based on Proposition D.1, the FDR control results below follows directly by the proof of Theorems 2.4–2.5.

Theorem D.2 (FDR control results for undirected networks)

Remark E.1 (Splitting procedure)

Note that when the missing rate qi,j∈[c,c′]q_{i,j}\in[c,c^{\prime}] for some c,c′∈[0,1)c,c^{\prime}\in[0,1), we typically have |ℐtesti0|≍n|{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}|\asymp n. If we split the train and calibration sets equally, we have |ℐtraini0|≍|ℐcalibi0|≍|ℐtesti0|≍n|{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}|\asymp|{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}|\asymp|{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}|\asymp n. This implies that in multiple splitting, we can only demand the size of each split |ℐcalibi0​(j0)|≈|ℐcalibi0|/|ℐtesti0|≍1|{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}(j_{0})|\approx|{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}|/|{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}|\asymp 1, i.e. , |ℐcalibi0​(j0)||{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}(j_{0})| is at a constant level. Such a constant size will lead to high randomness of multiple testing, but on the other hand, it can guarantee sufficient large number of fully observed rows Ωj0\Omega_{j_{0}} and thus maintain the estimation error as well as the power of selection. Moreover, when the missing values are scarce, we have small |ℐtesti0||{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}|. In this case, the splitting on ℐtesti0{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}} is not required, i.e. , ℐtesti0​(k0)=ℐtesti0{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}(k_{0})={\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}. Instead, we can split ℐcalibi0{\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}} into more than |ℐtesti0||{\cal I}_{\rm test}^{i_{0}}| sets such that the size of each subset is at a moderate level (to ensure enough fully observed rows in Ωj0\Omega_{j_{0}}), and apply e-BH using part of the subsets.

Moreover, we show that under structured missingness patterns, such as block or staggered missingness (Athey et al., 2021; Xiong and Pelger, 2023), there remain sufficiently many fully observed rows for each (i0,j0)(i_{0},j_{0}) under mild regularity conditions. We take block missingness as an illustrative example; the argument for staggered missingness follows analogously.

Proposition E.2 (Fully observed rows under block missingness)

Then, if choosing |ℐtraini0|=c2​n|{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}|=c_{2}n for some constant c2<c1c_{2}<c_{1}, we have |Ωj0|=|ℐtraini0|=c2​n|\Omega_{j_{0}}|=|{\cal I}_{\rm train}^{i_{0}}|=c_{2}n for each j0j_{0} and for any choice of ℐcalibi0​(j0){\cal I}_{\rm calib}^{i_{0}}(j_{0}).
